name: PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indo Tambangraya Megah: a net-cash, high-CV Kalimantan producer whose dividend no longer covers the tape premium
frontmatter.summary: ITM sells high-CV Kalimantan coal at a fixed-price-driven discount to the Newcastle marker, runs net cash and pays a variable dividend. The revision measures the current-year realised price on the six-month actual, prices the mine's strip and lifts the elapsed year out of the scenario shocks. On those inputs the base value and the weighted target sit below the tape, so we move to HOLD: the dividend no longer covers the premium the market pays over the mine's economic-life value.
thesis: The current year's realised price is measured on the six-month actual, not read off a stable-ratio assumption: two-thirds of the sales book is fixed-price, so a rising marker is not passed through at the prior-year ratio [S2, F26].

Volume is the company's own plan, not our call: the current-year line sits inside the published indicative sales range, is held near the top of it through the near term and then eases onto a flat line, because the stated reserve base supports well over a decade at that rate and nothing in the mine plan sources a fade [S2, S3].

The balance sheet is the hinge: net cash, a small debt line and a standing buyback authorisation mean the dividend and the capital return, not the FY2032E economic-life NAV, are what the market is capitalising [S0].

Costs follow the mine plan rather than the prior-year blend: the strip ratio is held at the six-month run-rate and the purchased-coal book is re-based to the gap between the sales target and the production target [S2, S3].

The scenarios mirror on the benchmark and now carry the one-stop export channel; the bear sizes its volume clip to the Indominco concession and the bull cannot mirror it upward because the work-plan quota caps output [S2].

FY2027 RKAB approval from ESDM; the quota sets next year's volume line

blocks.text: **What changed (31 October 2026).** This revision answers the first red-team round and the QC audit. The current-year realised price is re-based on the six-month actual, because with 67.0% of sales fixed-price a rising marker is not passed through at the old ratio [S2, F26]; that is the change that moves the rating. The strip ratio is held at the run-rate and then the slightly deeper quarterly print, not the prior-year average [S2]. The purchased-coal cost is rebuilt from the LK's cost note against the gap between the sales and production targets [S3, S2]. Discretionary expansion capex is no longer charged while the assets it funds are carried at nil [S2, S4]. The one-stop export rule of PP No. 24/2026 and Permendag No. 15/2026 is now a mirrored scenario shock, not only a risk entry, and the elapsed current year is lifted out of both market legs [S6]. Three citation errors are corrected: the controlling stake, the buyback window and the six-month EBITDA attribution [S3, S2]. The QC pass then fixed the IFRS 16 treatment: the bridge now uses the company's own 30 June 2026 cash and borrowings and charges the leases once through the operating cost base rather than also deducting the lease liability [S2, S3]; the EBITDA line is reconciled to the LK's presented figure [S5]; the valuation text is restated on the engine's FY2032E economic-life cut rather than the reserve life [S0]; and the bull's volume is capped at the top of the company's guided range [S2, F15].

We move coverage of PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk to **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of **Rp21,534** against a last price of Rp24,900: a total return of **-5.3%** on our probability-weighted scenarios, with the dividend no longer enough to carry the equity past the tape. The company is the Indonesian thermal-coal arm of the Banpu group: four CCoW concessions in East and Central Kalimantan plus a clutch of IUPs, producing a high-calorific-value product, with the Imm and Tcm coals well up the grade range [S2], sold to China, Japan, India and the domestic power market from a net-cash balance sheet [S3].

Our through-cycle NAV — cut at the FY2032E economic life, the year that maximises cumulative present value, not the full reserve life — is **Rp15,984**, below the tape, because the coal deck's long-run Newcastle marker mean-reverts below spot and we do not capitalise the war premium. The cut leaves 191.4 Mt of the 382 Mt reserve in the ground: beyond that year free cash flow at deck prices is negative, so carrying the tail would lower the value rather than raise it [S0]. The dividend method is what lifts the blended value above it: on the modelled payout the shares support a dividend-capacity yield capitalised at **Rp18,000** [S0], the anchor the market has paid for this name, though no longer enough to reach the price. Both cross-checks sit above the DCF — EV/EBITDA at Rp33,316 (108.4% above) and the dividend method at Rp18,000 (12.6% above) — so the blended value sits between the economic-life value and the market's multiple, below the tape.

The variant view: the tape implies the Newcastle benchmark holds near **US$132/t** through the horizon, a factor of 1.1 on the deck's first marker [S0], which we think is too generous on price and not too harsh on volume. Three things move the value: the benchmark, the RKAB quota that sets the volume line, and the domestic take under the standing cap [S2, S3].

PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk is an Indonesian thermal-coal producer, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2007 and now a subsidiary of Banpu Minerals (Singapore) Pte. Ltd., which holds 65.1% of the shares indirectly through Banpu Public Company Limited, with the balance in public hands and a small treasury position [S3, S2]. It reports in US dollars, sells in US dollars, and employs 1,609.0 people [S0]. The group's own structure slide shows the controlling chain — Banpu at roughly two thirds, the public at roughly a third, and a small treasury-share position [S2].

The business is a single commodity with a diversified mine portfolio: four CCoW concessions — Indominco Mandiri (CCOW Gen I, East Kalimantan), Trubaindo (Gen II), Bharinto Ekatama (Gen III) and Jorong Barutama Greston (Gen II, South Kalimantan) — plus four IUPs (Graha Panca Karsa, Tepian Indah Sukses, Nusa Persada Resources, Kitadin) [S3]. The product mix is skewed to the higher grades — Imm, Tcm and Bek — while Jbg, Gpk and Npr sit lower [S2]. That grade mix is what makes the realised price key off the Newcastle and HBA markers rather than the low-grade ICI indices [S2].

Alongside the coal book the group runs adjacent businesses that are small against it: coal trading through an energy-commodities subsidiary, mining contractor and port services, a barge port serving the Melak cluster, and a rooftop-solar arm [S2, S3], plus a mineral-sector vehicle stood up in October 2026 [S4]. None is material to value, and we no longer charge their expansion spend while crediting no return: no archived filing discloses segment revenue, a project value or a separable sunk capex for these assets, and the company reports no material capital commitments and no realised capital-goods investment for the year [S2, S3, S4]. We therefore exclude the discretionary capex from the coal cash flow and carry the optionality at nil, symmetrically, rather than at an invented number [S3].

The competitive position is a mid-sized, high-grade, low-cost Indonesian producer: a price-taker on the marker with a cost position in the first part of the global curve [S3]. Its reserve base was 382 Mt of JORC reserves at the end of 2025 [S3, F11]; on the production plan of 22.9 Mt that is a reserve life of roughly seventeen years. The DCF itself stops earlier, at the engine's maximum-cumulative-PV year of FY2032E, because the late-life free cash flow at deck prices turns negative; the valuation section explains why carrying the tail would reduce value rather than add it [S0]. The nearest expiry is the Indominco concession in March 2028, which is also the largest single production unit [S2].

Thermal coal is a cyclical, dollar-priced, policy-shaped commodity, and the deck we work from frames it that way: the Newcastle 6,000 kcal/kg marker is the price series, the DMO cap is the administered ceiling on domestic power tonnes, and the coal deck's long-run view is that the marginal Indonesian tonne clears in a band around its long-run marker once the war premium fades [S0]. Our industry read is that supply discipline, not demand growth, is what has held the price up: the company's own market commentary names Indonesian RKAB uncertainty and higher domestic-market obligations as the supply constraint, alongside logistics disruption in South Africa and Colombia and the war-driven diesel shortage in Russia, with Chinese domestic output and Indian import substitution the two demand-side dampeners [S2].

Regulation is the swing factor. Coal sits under the RKAB annual work-plan approval, which sets each producer's permitted volume, and under the domestic market obligation that reserves a share of output for the national power market at the administered cap [S2, S3]. The royalty regime depends on the licence: the CCoW mines pay a contract-specific rate and the IUP mines the lower schedule, and the royalty the group actually booked was 220 USD m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in the last year, below the contract headline [S3]. We set the licence to the work-agreement regime and the royalty to the booked effective rate, and justify both in the model.

The newest layer is the export channel. Exports of strategic resources must be handled by the state export company PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia from 1 January 2027, under PP No. 24/2026 and Permendag No. 15/2026 [S6]. The coal Eksportir Terdaftar licence is valid only to 31 December 2026; after that the state exporter is the only permitted channel, and producers must report export documents and contracts to it through an integrated system [S6]. APBI warns that treating it as a formality could leave coal unable to be exported on 1 January 2027 [S6]. The export base is 19.2 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold in the last year [S3, F21]. The exposure is process rather than price — nothing reported sets a fee or a different realised price — so we size it as a small mirrored shipment-timing shock in the scenarios.

The moat is grade and cost position rather than scale: a high-CV product with a first-quartile cash cost is what survives a trough, and ITM's strip ratio and unit cost sit in that part of the curve [S3]. Its pricing power is nil on the marker and real on the mix — but the mix cuts both ways, and the previous edition overstated the pass-through: because 67.0% of current-year sales are fixed-price and only a quarter indexed, a move in the marker reaches the realised price with a lag, and the ratio falls when the marker rises [S2, F26]. That is what the six-month print shows, and why we measure the ratio on the latest actual. On the five forces, supplier power is moderate (contract mining and fuel, with diesel the live cost pressure), buyer power is high, substitutes are real but slow — with gas-to-coal switching in Japan, Korea and Taiwan holding thermal demand firm [S2] — new entrants are gated by permits, capital and the RKAB, and rivalry is disciplined by the same regime.

The five-year record is a classic coal cycle. Revenue ran at US$3,636.2m in the peak year, fell to US$2,374.3m and US$2,304.5m, and reached US$1,881.1m in the last actual year [S0, S3]. The compression is entirely price: volumes were steady at 24.0 and 24.7 of sales tonnage in the last two years [S3], while the realised price fell from 95.7 to 76.0 [S5]. Gross margin narrowed with it, and net profit to parent fell to US$190.9m [S0].

Our forecast rebuilds the same way: revenue is volume times a capped realised price, with volume the company's own current-year range held flat [S2], and the realised price the deck's Newcastle marker times a ratio measured on the six-month actual for the current year and fitted on the last two completed years thereafter, because the fixed book rolls off [S5, S2]. That gives first-forecast-year revenue of US$2,203.5m at a realised price of 81.0, the six-month actual held into the full year and above the 76.0 of last year, and an EBITDA of US$293.6m that reproduces the last actual year on more tonnes, with the deeper strip and the larger purchased-coal book absorbing the price gain [S0, S2 p.21].

Costs are where caution usually creeps in, and we have kept it out. Cash cost per tonne is the physical strip ratio times the mining cost per cubic metre, backed out of the LK's cost-of-revenue note, plus a residual for hauling, barging, processing and the purchased-coal book [S3]. The strip is held at the six-month run-rate because the company's quarterly disclosure has the pits deepening and the ratio guided higher at the two largest mines [S2]. The purchased book is rebuilt, not inherited: mining costs of 653.3 US$m and coal purchases of 256.3 US$m sit in the LK note [S3], and the gap between the sales target and the production target implies more purchased tonnes than the prior-year mix [S2]. Royalty is the booked effective rate, not the contract headline [S3], and SG&A is held at the last actual's share of revenue because the step-up reads as structural [S3].

We restate depreciation rather than model around it: the pack's prior-year figure is a stub because the cash-flow statement uses the direct method, so we take the LK's own charge for the last two years and let the engine rebuild history [S3]. The line we carry is the property, plant and equipment depreciation charged to cost of revenue; right-of-use depreciation is treated as an operating cost and sits in the selling and G&A lines the unit-cost build reconciles to [S3]. That is why our last-year EBITDA (operating income plus that PPE charge) sits below the company's presented EBITDA of 343 USD m: the company adds back total D&A, of which right-of-use depreciation is 36.9 USD m [S5 p.23, S3]. The gap is a definitional lease treatment, not a cost we have missed, and the 35.5 USD m of cash lease payments in the LK's cash-flow statement bears it out [S3]. We do not add the right-of-use charge back a second time, and we do not deduct the lease liability from equity.

The bridge uses the company's own 30 June 2026 balance sheet: cash of 738 USD m against borrowings of 18.0 USD m, a net-cash position [S2]. The data pack's larger cash and debt lines are not used. Its debt line is total debt including lease liabilities, and the lease component is a derived residual — the pack's total-debt line less the company's borrowings — not a figure the company discloses line-by-line at the interim date. The last disclosed lease liability was 40.4 USD m current plus 9.8 USD m non-current at 31 December 2025 [S3 p.142]; the increase to the interim date is an inference from the new vessel, port and mine leases signed since, not a filing figure, and the valuation does not rest on it. The pack's cash line does not tie to the interim disclosure either, so the two balance sheets are reconciled by adopting the company's [S2, S3 p.142]. Capex is sustaining spend per tonne, held flat in nominal terms; the LK's total reconciles as 79.0 USD m of property, plant and equipment purchases plus 40.7 USD m of deferred exploration and development (the deferred-stripping build) [S3], and the six-month run-rate is well below the prior-year average [S2]. Discretionary expansion spend is excluded for the business-section reason [S3, S2, S4]. Working capital is thin and held at the historical ratio, and no new borrowing is assumed [S0, S2].

Earnings quality. ITM is clean. On the card's accruals test, net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets is negative — operating cash flow of 285.5 US$m exceeded net profit of US$194.7m in the last year, and the prior year shows the same sign [S0, S3] — so earnings are cash-backed and receivables fell on lower prices [S0]. There is no special-notation or special-board flag; the shares trade in the main market and the LK is audited and unqualified [S3]. Related-party gravity is low and quantified: coal sales to related parties were under 1.0% of net revenue and related-party marketing about a tenth of selling expenses, disclosed and arm's length [S3, F30]. The controlling holder has roughly two thirds, the buyback is authorised but unsized so we assume no share reduction, and there is no rights-issue or discounted-placement pattern [S3, S2]. One optics-class flag: the variable dividend is a board decision, carried at the LK's latest rate [S0, S3].

Indonesian thermal coal producers have historically been valued less on the life of their reserves than on the cash they return, because the reserve life is long relative to the policy horizon and the cash-return decision is annual.

We value ITM on the house method for commodity producers: a through-cycle discounted cash flow over the mine's economic life as the primary method, an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a dividend-capacity cross-check, weighted **60.0%**, **25.0%** and **15.0%** [S0]. The fit is that the value is a finite, price-taking cash-flow stream: a cyclical producer should never be valued on spot earnings, and the primary DCF runs the mine's finite life at the deck's through-cycle prices with no terminal value, cut at the FY2032E maximum-cumulative-PV year rather than carried to reserve depletion [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house inputs: a risk-free rate of 5.0%, a mature-market premium of 4.2%, a country premium of 2.5%, and an unlevered beta of 0.80 lifting to 0.81 levered at the statutory tax rate of 22.0% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of **10.4%** and a WACC of **10.3%** [S0]. We carry no governance premium: related-party flows are small and there is no controlling-stake pledge on the register [S3].

The primary method gives **Rp15,984** per share, below the tape, and the reason is the deck, not the company: the long-run marker is flat in real terms and well below spot, the war premium is a cycle position, and the realised price is a fraction of the marker [S0]. The DCF runs on sales tonnes, so the purchased book draws down the reserve statement, and the engine stops at FY2032E — the year that maximises cumulative present value on the modelled path [S0]. That is the economic life, not the reserve life: the reserve depletes around FY2039E, leaving 191.4 Mt of the 382 Mt base still in the ground at the cut, but free cash flow is negative in every year from FY2033E to FY2039E at the deck's prices, so the omitted tail is value-negative and carrying it would reduce the NAV rather than add to it — excluding it lifts the DCF by roughly two per cent. Net of the small debt line, the enterprise value is 261.8 [S0].

The cross-checks diverge, and the divergence is the point. EV/EBITDA gives **Rp33,316**, 108.4% above the primary, because the peer multiple blends names trading on a war-premium cash flow [S0]. The dividend method gives **Rp18,000**, 12.6% above, because it capitalises the annual cash return at a yield the market has accepted rather than the economic-life value [S0]. We carry both at their house weights: the market is paying for the cash return, and the economic-life value is the floor beneath it. The EV/EBITDA leg is a re-rating to a war-premium peer multiple rather than a through-cycle value — on ITM's own five-year average multiple instead of the peer-blended one, the leg would sit only a little above the DCF, so the range, not the blended number, is the cross-check [S0].

What the price implies: run the DCF backwards and the tape requires the Newcastle benchmark near **US$132/t**, a factor of 1.1 on the deck's first marker [S0]. That embeds the war premium persisting, a low-yield dividend capitalisation and no policy surprise. We do not think the premium persists on the current-year economics, and our target sits below the price because the dividend and the probability-weighted near-term cash return no longer cover the gap between the tape and the economic-life value.

The downside risks. **Regulatory** (medium likelihood, high impact): the RKAB cycle sets the volume line and the domestic obligation diverts tonnes to the capped power market [S2]. **Concession** (medium, high): the Indominco CCoW expires in March 2028 and is the largest single production unit with the thinnest reserve base, so an onerous extension hits volume and royalty [S2]. **Export channel** (medium, medium): from 1 January 2027 coal may be exported only through PT DSI, and APBI warns an unprepared transition could stall shipments [S6]; we size it as a small realised-price clip in the bear and its mirror in the bull. **Macro** (medium, high): the complex carries a war premium and the deck sees the long-run marker well below spot, so mean reversion is the base case [S0]. **FX** (low, medium): dollar revenue against a partly rupiah cost base [S3]. **Operational** (medium, medium): the mine plan raises the strip ratio as pits deepen [S2]. **Governance and liquidity** (low, low): related-party flows are small, there is no pledge, and the shares are liquid [S3, S0]. **Capital allocation** (low, medium): the buyback is unsized, its window runs only to 4 November 2026, and the shares trade above reserve NAV, so execution above that line transfers value [S3].

Our scenarios are mirrored on the benchmark, the capped domestic share and a small realised-price clip, and we have not stacked the bear. The price shocks are specified as a symmetric full-cycle move from FY2027, the house default, but because the engine multiplies the whole forecast, each leg uses the present-value-equivalent uniform multiplier: the elapsed current year, three-quarters actual and at the reviewed spot, is not shocked, and the tail carries the full move. The bear raises the domestic take, clips a small slice of the realised price for the export-channel transition, and sizes the volume clip to the Indominco concession: the mine is 7.1 Mt of the 22.9 Mt current-year production plan [S2], holds 31.0 Mt of reserves and its CCoW expires in March 2028 [S2], so a failed extension removes about three-tenths of mined volume. Because the engine shocks the whole forecast, the volume clip is likewise a present-value equivalent. The bull is the mirror on the benchmark, the domestic take and the export clip, and runs volume at the top of the company's own guided sales range rather than above it; it cannot mirror the bear's volume cut upward because the work-plan quota and the guidance cap output [S2, F15], so it earns its return from price rather than from invented volume. Neither leg shocks the required return or the royalty rate, and a failed extension's move toward the step royalty schedule is stated as a further downside rather than shocked [S3].

On those shocks the bear is **Rp17,691**, the bull **Rp28,567** and the base **Rp20,723**, at probabilities of 0.25, 0.55 and 0.20 [S0]. The bull carries a smaller weight than the bear because its volume upside is capped by the company's own guidance while the bear's Indominco mechanism is a live concession expiry; the price legs themselves are mirrored, and the macro desk is neutral on thermal coal with the deck flagging spot as a war-premium carry, not a level [S0]. The base dominates because the most probable path is the company's own plan at the deck's prices.

The rating is not presented as more robust than it is. The base value of **Rp20,723** is below the last price of Rp24,900, so the base price-only return is negative and the total return stays negative even after the dividend; only the bull clears the tape. With the bear weight doubled and the bull cut correspondingly the probability-weighted value would sit further below the last price, which is why we do not underwrite the target on the bull's convexity. The HOLD is a valuation call: the dividend is no longer enough to cover the premium the tape pays over the value of the mine's economic life, and a lower entry would be needed to make the total return positive. The signposts that would change the view: an RKAB outcome below the indicative range; a domestic obligation above the current share; whether the export channel clears coal without a shipment gap in early 2027 [S6]; a sustained marker move either side of the deck path; the Indominco extension terms; and a new and better-priced buyback authorisation.

Ownership is straightforward. Banpu Minerals (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. holds 65.1% indirectly through Banpu Public Company Limited, with the public holding the balance and a small treasury position [S3, S2]. The register shows no pledged controlling stake and no margin-call structure [S3]. The audit is unqualified and the accounts carry the coal-specific royalty and stripping disclosures the sector needs [S3].

On related parties, coal sales to related parties were under 1.0% of net revenue and related-party marketing about a tenth of selling expenses, disclosed and arm's length [S3, F30]. We found no discounted placement, no serial rights issue and no auditor down-tier change. The buyback is capped at a share of paid-up capital but its window ends on 4 November 2026, so it is a closing capital-return decision [S3].

The dividend record is variable: the LK's payout-ratio disclosure shows the group distributing of the order of three-fifths of each year's profit with no formulaic floor [S0, S3], which we carry at the latest rate. On ESG, the group's own disclosure is above the sector median on the third-party scores it cites, with emissions work on biodiesel substitution and grid power and rehabilitation on post-mining forest return [S2]. A thermal-coal producer carries an unavoidable transition discount; what is controllable is capital discipline and reclamation, and both read as adequate [S2, S3].

The dated catalysts are the third-quarter operational release (sales against the indicative FY2026 range, the realised price against the six-month actual, the strip against guidance), the FY2027 RKAB approval that sets next year's volume, the 1 January 2027 switch to the state export channel which is the first live test of whether tonnes clear [S6], the annual general meeting that declares the final dividend and considers a new buyback authorisation, and the Indominco expiry in the medium term [S2, S3].

Between updates we monitor the sector dashboard's KPIs: sales volume against the range; the realised price against the deck, re-checked every quarter; the strip ratio and unit cash cost against the mine plan; the booked royalty rate, the cleanest early signal of a regime change; EBITDA per tonne; reserves, which set the horizon; net debt, which stays negative; the payout ratio, the market's anchor; and, from January 2027, the export share cleared through the state exporter and any transition delay [S0, S3, S6]. The royalty rate and the reserve statement matter most, because either would re-price the model or change how long it runs. The fixed-price book means the realisation ratio moves with the direction of the marker, so a shift of more than a few points is the single assumption most likely to be wrong in either direction.

bear.narrative: The war premium unwinds and overshoots: the bear takes the deck's Newcastle path down 20% from FY2027 - the house default and the mirror of the bull - a demand-led trough through the marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names as the level at which marginal Indonesian supply clears. FY2026 is NOT shocked: the year is three-quarters elapsed at the reviewed spot, so the whole-forecast multiplier is set at 0.91, which at the model's price-path weights is the PV-equivalent of holding the elapsed year at the deck and applying 0.8 from FY2027 (about 55% of the price-path PV sits in FY2026). The volume shock is now sized to the Indominco Mandiri concession, not a generic clip: IMM is 7.1 Mt of the 22.2 Mt FY26 production plan [S2, F27, F28], holds only 31 Mt of reserves [S2, F29] and its CCoW Gen I expires in March 2028 [S2], so a failed extension removes about three-tenths of mined volume; the engine applies shocks to the whole forecast, so the banked clip is the PV-equivalent loss across the horizon. The government also raises the share of tonnes diverted to the capped domestic power market. A small additional realised-price clip carries the one-stop export transition (PP No. 24/2026, state exporter PT DSI from January 2027 [S6]): a first-quarter shipment gap through the new channel, mirrored in the bull. A failed IMM extension on onerous terms could also move the contract mines toward the IUPK step schedule and lift the booked royalty [S3]; we state that as a further downside rather than shock it, because the royalty rate is set by contract and government schedule. The lower benchmark with the LK-rate payout cuts the dividend mechanically, so the bear value and the dividend cut arrive together. No re-rating or required-return shock is taken.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same four drivers: the war premium holds and Chinese mine-safety curbs plus Indonesian RKAB discipline keep seaborne supply tight into 2027, so the benchmark runs 20% above the deck's path from FY2027 and ITM's high-CV Kalimantan coals capture the premium in full; FY2026 is held at the reviewed spot rather than shocked (the whole-forecast multiplier of 1.09 is the PV-equivalent of the elapsed year at the deck plus 1.2 from FY2027, and puts the FY2026 marker at about the US$150.4 reviewed spot [S0]); the export-channel transition clears without a shipment gap, so the realised-price clip reverses; volumes run at the TOP of the company's own guided sales range (27.5 of a 27.2 Mt base), not above it, because no archived source quantifies Bunyut throughput or an NPR uplift; and the domestic-market take eases back as export economics improve. The volume asymmetry against the bear is deliberate and sourced: upside is capped by the RKAB and the company's own 26.9-27.5 Mt sales target [S2, F15], so a symmetric three-tenths uplift is not physically available and the bull earns its return from price. The probability weight is cut to reflect the smaller volume upside. The royalty rate and the required return are NOT shocked: no sourced mechanism lets the booked royalty rate fall, and a bull that assumes a re-rating would be a defect. The standing buyback authorisation is a capital-return lever only if executed below reserve NAV; the shares trade about two-fifths above it, so no buyback credit is taken [S3, F20].

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own published target, not our guess: the 2Q26 analyst presentation puts FY26 indicative coal sales at 26.9-27.5 Mt [S2, F15] against FY2025 actual sales of 24.7 Mt [S3, F1] and 6M26 sales of 12.3 Mt [S2]. The step-up is sourced and structural rather than a market call: sales run well above production (FY2026 production target is 22.0-22.9 Mt against a 26.9-27.5 Mt sales target [S2]) because the group draws down ROM and stockpile inventory and resells purchased coal through its trading arm, so the FY2026 sales line is the company's, held near the midpoint. FY2027E-FY2030E are held broadly FLAT rather than faded: the 382 Mt reserve base [S3, F11] supports roughly fourteen years at this run-rate and nothing in the mine plan [S2] sources a decline, and the most-likely rule forbids an unsourced volume fade. The reserves cap in the template, not a stylised fade, is what ends the volume line.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: RE-BASED ON THE 6M26 ACTUAL, not on a lagged H1 ratio. FY2026E 0.614 is set so that the engine reproduces the company's own six-month realised price: at the deck's FY2026E Newcastle marker (US$137.0), 0.78 x 0.614 x 137.0 + 0.22 x 70.0 = US$81.0/t, which is exactly the 6M26 ASP [S2 p.21] (F16 is the 2Q26 print of US$82.7/t, not the six-month figure). The previous 0.655 was the raw H1 ratio (US$81.0 over the H1-2026 average of about US$128.9) applied to a full-year marker 6% above the H1 level, which implicitly required an H2 ASP step-up that the contract book does not support: 67% of FY26 sales are fixed-price and only 24% indexed [S2, F26], so only about a quarter of the book can respond to a rising marker within the year. Holding the current year at the six-month actual is the most-likely read, not a haircut: it is the last actual, and the fixed two-thirds is locked. FY2027E-FY2030E revert to 0.7167, the ratio fitted on the last two completed fiscal years (FY2025A ASP US$76.0/t [S5, F3] over the deck's US$108.4 = 0.701; FY2024A US$95.7/t [S5, F4] over US$136.1 = 0.703, lifted to 0.7167 for the 22% capped domestic share), because the fixed 2026 book rolls off and the two-actual level is the through-cycle anchor. ITM's realised price is structurally below the Newcastle 6,000 marker: the product is a blend of 5,600-6,200 kcal/kg GAR (IMM) and higher-CV TCM/BEK coals [S2, F17], a fifth of tonnes go to the domestic market at HBA/DMO-linked prices [S3, F12], and the method card has Indonesian coal key off HBA/ICI rather than Newcastle. The FY2025A calibration gate is answered in qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda: it re-prices history at the FY2026E ratio, a forecast-year measurement, not a mis-specified cost base.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: The company's own disclosed domestic share: 5.5 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold in FY2025 went to the Indonesian domestic market [S3, F12], i.e. 22.3% of sales volume, and those tonnes settle at HBA/DMO-linked prices against the standing US$70/t power cap carried in the coal deck (d.coal.dmo_cap). We hold 22% of tonnes under the cap rather than ramping it: the DMO is a fixed government share of production (25% of output for domestic supply), and ITM's disclosed domestic share has been stable, so a rising domestic take is a policy risk stated in §5 rather than a modelled drift. Capped tonnes receive min(cap, realised price), which bites hardest in the bull case.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Carried as the PHYSICAL overburden-to-coal ratio (bcm/t) on the AADI/GEMS/BUMI peer convention, so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm is the mining block per tonne and is directly comparable with the other COAL names. FY2026E is set at the 6M26 actual of 10.3x [S2, F18], not the FY2025A full-year average of 9.4x [S3, F7]: the group printed 10.3x in 6M26 (1Q26 10.4x, 2Q26 10.3x against 6M25 9.3x) [S2, F18], with IMM guided to 14.0x and TCM to 17.6x in 3Q26 as the pits deepen [S2], offset by BEK's lower 7.7-8.6x. Pricing the first forecast year at the FY2025A average would price a cost base the mine plan has already left behind. The path holds the current run-rate and then the slightly deeper 10.4x actually printed in 1Q26 [S2, F18] for the rest of the forecast, carrying the guided deepening rather than reverting to the prior-year average; it does not compound further, because the reserve statement [S3, F11] gives no basis for a permanent climb and the per-mine 3Q26 guides (IMM 14.0x, TCM 17.6x) are offset by BEK's lower 7.7-8.6x [S2]. The engine's calibration gap is therefore the difference between this run-rate strip and the FY2025A average, justified under qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: The overburden-removal and coal-getting cost per bank cubic metre. Backed out of the LK's own cost-of-revenue note: mining costs of US$653.3m on 24.7 Mt sold [S3, F1] is US$26.45/t, and at the FY2025A strip ratio of 9.4x [S3, F7] that is US$2.81/bcm — inside the US$2.6-8.0/bcm band the peer COAL names book, which is the check that the axis means the same thing across the deck. It escalates with the USD deck thereafter rather than falling in real terms, because the company names rising diesel and contract-mining rates as the live cost pressure (the presentation shows fuel at US$0.99/litre in 6M26 against US$0.78 a year earlier [S2]) and nothing in the filings sources a real decline.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Residual per-tonne cash cost ex-royalty and ex-D&A, rebuilt on the LK's own cost-of-revenue note rather than held at the FY2025 blend. The FY2025A anchor: cost of revenue of US$1,398.3m [S0] less royalty of US$220.0m [S3, F10] less depreciation of US$26.9m [S3, F8], over 24.7 Mt sold [S3, F1] = US$46.6/t ex-royalty ex-D&A; of that, mining costs were US$653.3m [S3, F24], coal purchases US$256.3m [S3, F23] and the rest transportation, salaries, forestry fees, repairs, fuel and reclamation [S3]. The purchased-coal volume is the round-1 fix: FY2026 sales of 27.2 Mt against a production target of 22.0-22.9 Mt [S2, F28] implies about 4.75 Mt of purchased coal against about 3.5 Mt in FY2025, so purchases rise by roughly US$90m at the LK's US$73/t. That is NOT added in full, because the strip block above is charged on sales tonnes and already rises with the deeper pits: bottom-up, total cash cost is about US$49.6/t (mining about US$735m spread over 27.2 Mt sold, purchases about US$348m, other about US$266m), and at the modelled 10.3x strip and US$2.81/bcm the mining block contributes US$28.9/t, leaving US$20.7/t here - up from US$20.17 on the FY2025 mix. Supporting SG&A is NOT put here: ITM's selling and administrative expenses run at 11.5% of revenue, which the engine carries separately in opex_pct. Escalated gently with services and labour inflation.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK notes, not the data pack. ITM's consolidated depreciation of property, plant and equipment charged to cost of revenue was US$26.86m in FY2025 and US$38.71m in FY2024 [S3, F8, F9]. The pack's FY2025A D&A of US$32.5m is in the right region but its FY2024A figure of US$1.3m is a stub, because the IDX cash-flow statement is presented on the direct method and carries no D&A add-back — which is exactly the restatement the method card asks for. THE RIGHT-OF-USE TREATMENT IS DELIBERATE AND IS NOT AN OMISSION: ROU depreciation was US$36.9m in FY2025 (US$32.5m of it in selling expenses [S3, F32]) and the ROU asset balance rose from US$3.0m to US$47.1m as new vessel, port and mine leases were capitalised [S3, F38]. We do NOT add that back here: the leases are treated as an operating cost, the cost lines the unit build reconciles to already carry the ROU depreciation, and the US$35.5m of cash lease payments [S3, F33] matches it. Adding ROU back to EBITDA/FCFF while also choosing to pay the lease cash out of the same cost base would double-count. This is why the model's FY2025A EBITDA (US$293.5m = operating income + PPE depreciation in cost of revenue) sits below the company's presented EBITDA of US$343.1m, which adds the total D&A of US$76.2m back [S5 p.23]: the difference is ROU depreciation plus the ~US$12m of other depreciation/amortisation that sits in the cost lines. Held at the FY2025A rate of US$1.09/t thereafter on the flat volume path.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Sustaining capital only. The FY2025 capex of US$119.7m on the data pack reconciles to the LK cash-flow statement as US$79.0m of property, plant and equipment purchases plus US$40.7m of deferred exploration and development (the deferred-stripping build) [S3, F36, F37], i.e. US$4.85/t total. Both legs are sustaining-grade spend tied to the mine: the deferred stripping is a direct function of the strip ratio, and the Bunyut/solar/mineral spend disclosed in the annual report has no separable dollar figure and no material-commitment note [S3 p.151], so it cannot be quantified out. The per-tonne line is nevertheless set at US$4.00/t, not US$4.85/t, because the most recent run-rate is materially lower: 6M26 capex was US$21m against US$32m in 6M25 [S2 p.23], an annualised ~US$42m, so US$4.00/t already sits ABOVE the current run-rate and only below the prior-year average that carried a large deferred-stripping addition. The discretionary expansion projects are not charged separately (capex_other is nil) and are carried at nil symmetrically. Held FLAT in nominal terms thereafter; the most-likely rule holds costs at the last actual in real terms and nothing sources a real rise.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: EXCLUDED from FCFF after the round-1 challenge. The previous build charged the Bunyut port capacity works, the solar pipeline (152 MWp contracted, 86 MWp operating at 2Q26 [S2, F31]) and the new mineral-sector vehicle ITM Mineral Investama [S4] through free cash flow while setting other_revenue to zero and carrying the assets at nil - a one-sided cost. No archived filing discloses segment revenue or a project value for any of them, and the most-likely rule forbids inventing one, so the discretionary expansion spend is removed from the coal DCF and the optionality is carried at nil rather than charged and ignored. Sustaining capex continues to carry the mine's own spend, and the port and solar works that serve the Melak cluster sit inside the operating cost base the LK reports. A sourced revenue or project value would add value; none exists in the record, and the bull adds nothing here for the same reason.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company pays out a variable share of net profit — its stated policy is to distribute part of each year's profit as cash dividend after allowing for reserves and the development plan [S3]. The LK's own payout-ratio disclosure is the guide, not a DPS/EPS series: the FY2025 annual report's dividend table states a payout ratio of 60% for the latest year and 64% for the prior year [S3, p.157], and the AGMS minutes put the FY2024 distribution at 65% of that year's net profit and FY2023 at 65% [S3, p.171/179] — a 60-65% record. The DPS/EPS arithmetic the pack carries (Rp992 in FY2025, Rp2,983 in FY2024) misleads because the pack's DPS is the dividend PAID during the year against the prior year's profit, so it mixes the payment lag with the cycle. We use the LK's own latest rate, 60% — the last actual, which the base case reproduces — rather than the engine's three-year average of dividends paid over prior-year profit. The dividend is the anchor IDX coal names trade on, so the payout is also the market's own capitalisation rate and is cross-checked against dividend-capacity yield in §4.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The primary DCF runs to the end of the reserve life with no terminal value, so this scalar only feeds the EV/EBITDA and implied-multiple cross-checks. It is set at zero because a thermal-coal cash-flow stream should not carry perpetual real growth — the coal deck's long-run Newcastle marker is flat in real terms at US$105/t [S0].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: ITM's selling and general and administrative expenses were US$171m and US$45m in FY2025 [S3], 11.5% of net revenue, against US$178m and US$37m in FY2024, 9.3%. The step-up is structural (higher fuel and oil in selling, and rising mine-administration cost [S3]), so we hold the FY2025A level rather than the three-year average, which is pulled down by the FY2023 low cost base. Held flat thereafter in nominal terms.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: The effective rate the LK books, not the 13.5% CCoW headline: royalty expense was US$220.0m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in FY2025 (11.7%) and US$260.2m on US$2,304.5m in FY2024 (11.3%) [S3, F10]. That blend is the contract rate on the four CCoW/PKP2B mines (IMM Gen I, TCM and JBG Gen II, BEK Gen III) with the far lower IUP schedule on the IUP mines (GPK, TIS, NPR, Kitadin), plus the fact that the resold purchased-coal book carries no royalty — which is why a flat 11.7%, not 13.5%, reproduces what the group actually pays. Double-count check: royalty is inside the reported cost of revenue, so the mining block and other_cost_unit are set EX-ROYALTY and the engine adds royalty back as a separate percentage of revenue, counting the line once.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a real and rising cost pressure — the presentation shows diesel at US$0.99/litre in 6M26 against US$0.78 in 6M25 and names rising diesel and global inflation as a cost driver [S2] — but most of ITM's hauling, barging and contract mining is bought at unit rates that already embed the contractor's own diesel, so only a minority of the cost base is directly exposed. We set 15% rather than the 30% template convention, and give the reason: the oil deck's long-run Brent is a seeded, war-premium value, and passing a perpetual war premium through mining costs while the coal deck mean-reverts toward US$105/t would manufacture a margin squeeze that neither deck asserts.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: The renewable and mining-services lines are immaterial next to the coal book (solar capacity of 152 MWp contracted at 2Q26 [S2]) and are carried inside the coal revenue build, so no separate other-revenue line is modelled.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Template constant 10%; the non-coal lines are immaterial to group value.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: ITM is in a net-cash position — cash of US$738m against BORROWINGS of US$18m at 30 June 2026, i.e. net cash of US$720m, with the company reporting net gearing of negative 37% and debt-to-equity of 0.01x [S2, F34, F35] — so no new borrowing is assumed. The data pack's US$804.0m cash / US$99.3m debt is NOT used: its debt line is total debt including roughly US$81m of lease liabilities, and that lease component is a DERIVED residual (the pack's US$99.339m less the company's US$18.0m borrowings), not a disclosed 30 June 2026 figure. The last disclosed lease liability was US$50.153m at 31 December 2025 (US$40.351m current plus US$9.802m non-current [S3 p.142]); the six-month increase is an inference from new vessel, port and mine leases signed since, not a filing figure, and the valuation does not depend on it. Its cash line does not tie to the company's interim disclosure (see section 3). Leases are treated as an operating cost, not as debt: the LK already charges US$36.9m of right-of-use depreciation through selling and G&A expenses [S3, F32], and the US$35.5m of cash lease payments [S3, F33] shows the cost base pays for the leases, so deducting the lease liability from equity as well would count the same obligation twice. Any buyback is funded from internal cash [S3, F20].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: ITM's non-operating line is dominated by finance income on its large net-cash balance, which the engine computes separately via cash_yield; no separate non-operating items are assumed.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Share count is held at the reported level; the only movement is the treasury-stock position of 2.4% of its own shares held at 30 June 2026 [S2] and the buyback authorised to a maximum of 10% of paid-up capital at the 2025 AGMS [S3, F20]. Because the buyback is discretionary and unsized, no reduction in the share count is assumed in the base case.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default carried from history (S0): the three-year average of net working capital over revenue. ITM's working capital is thin and mostly inventory and prepaid taxes, so this is a small drag and is held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0): the three-year average effective rate, close to the Indonesian statutory 22% but lifted by the non-deductible items and the forestry/reclamation charges. Held flat; a different realised price would not move the statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). With borrowings of only US$18m against US$738m of cash at 30 June 2026 [S2, F34, F35] the cost of debt is not a value driver and the default is carried unchanged. The pack's US$99.3m debt line includes lease liabilities and is not used here.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). ITM holds a large net-cash balance and earns finance income of about US$40m a year on it (S0, S3), consistent with a low-single-digit treasury yield.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0): minority interests take a small share of net profit, consistent with the reported non-controlling interest balance and the 99.99% ownership of the producing subsidiaries [S2].

challenges.challenge: The realised price is the model's largest lever and the latest actual contradicts the calibration. FY2026E ASP of US$92.0 is 13.6% above the 6M26 actual of US$81.0 and 11.2% above 2Q26's US$82.7 (S2 p.21), against a 2Q26 NEX of US$135.4 and a 1H26 average of ~US$128.9. At the calibrated 0.717 the model would print ~US$91 at that 2Q26 benchmark; the company printed US$82.7, implying a blended realisation near 0.61-0.63. The presentation also discloses that 67% of FY26 sales are FIXED-price and only 24% indexed (S2 p.12), so the report's claim that "a given move in the Newcastle marker passes through to ITM's realised price at a stable ratio" is not what the evidence says. The FY2026E line requires a 25% second-half ASP jump (H2 101 vs H1 81) from a book that is two-thirds fixed.
challenges.answer: Re-calibrated the current-year realisation on the latest actuals and re-ran. FY2026E realisation is now 0.614, set so the engine lands on the company's own 6M26 ASP of US$81.0/t at the deck's FY2026E Newcastle marker of US$137.0: 0.78 x 0.614 x 137.0 + 0.22 x 70.0 = US$81.0/t. The old 0.655 applied the H1 ratio to a full-year marker 6% above the H1 level and implicitly required an H2 step-up that the two-thirds fixed book does not support; the H1 lag does not reverse in H2 because 67% of FY26 sales are fixed-price and only 24% indexed. FY2027E onward reverts to the two-actual 0.7167 as the fixed book rolls off. This is the change that moves the rating from ADD to HOLD.

challenges.section: 3. Financial analysis and forecasts / 5. Investment risks
challenges.challenge: The FY2026E strip ratio is held at 10.0x, below the 6M26 actual of 10.3x (S2 p.15) and well below the company's own 3Q26 guidance of 14.0x at IMM and 17.6x at TCM (S2 pp.16-17), and the path is then capped at 10.0x for eleven years. Section 3 says costs "follow the mine plan's stripping sequence", which the model does not do; and the -15% calibration gap is itself justified by the pits deepening. The two statements cannot both stand.
challenges.answer: FY2026E is carried at the 6M26 actual of 10.3x and the explicit path now holds 10.4x (the 1Q26 actual) through FY2030E and the long run rather than reverting toward the FY2025A 9.4x. The 3Q26 per-mine guides (IMM 14.0x, TCM 17.6x) are carried rather than ignored: they are offset by BEK's 7.7-8.6x, and no group-level path above 10.4x is sourced, so the per-mine deepening is reflected in the run-rate without inventing a permanent climb. Section 3 now says the strip follows the mine plan's deepening, and the calibration gap is the run-rate against the prior-year average.

challenges.challenge: The 2.5 Mt volume uplift from 24.7 to 27.2 Mt is sold at the full modelled ASP, but the cost build is per SOLD tonne and the residual (US$20.17/t) embeds the FY2025 mix of 3.5 Mt of purchased coal at ~US$73/t (S3 p.401 - coal purchases US$256.3m; mining costs US$653.3m on 21.2 Mt production). The FY26 sales target of 26.9-27.5 Mt against the 22.0-22.9 Mt production target (S2 p.15) implies ~5 Mt of purchases, so the residual should rise to ~US$23/t, not stay flat at US$20.17. The incremental 1.5 Mt of purchased coal carries ~US$80-110m of cost that the model does not book (partly offset by mining cost being spread over more sales tonnes, net ~US$45-90m, 8-16% of modelled EBITDA), and it persists every year of the forecast.
challenges.answer: The purchased book is re-based rather than inherited. The residual rises from the FY2025A 20.17/t to 20.7/t and the mining block is charged on sales tonnes at the deeper strip; total cash cost is about US$50/t against US$46.6/t in FY2025, with about 4.75 Mt of purchased coal at the LK's US$73/t (FY2026 sales of 27.2 Mt against the 22.0-22.9 Mt production target). Supporting SG&A stays in opex_pct, so it is not double-counted. The build is now on the same sales-tonne basis the engine uses and reconciles to the LK's cost-of-revenue note.

challenges.challenge: The regulation that triggered this update - coal exports only through the state exporter PT DSI from 1 January 2027, with Eksportir Terdaftar permits expiring 31 December 2026 (S6) - is absent from every scenario. The report itself rates it "medium likelihood, medium impact", says it is "the item most likely to cause a near-term volume miss", and notes APBI's warning that coal may not be exportable on day one; yet the bear carries no export-channel shock and the bull carries no mirror. The 19.2 Mt export book is the exposure.
challenges.answer: The one-stop export channel is now a scenario driver, not only a risk entry. Both legs carry a small mirrored realised-price clip (0.98 bear, 1.02 bull) for a first-quarter shipment gap through the state channel from January 2027, and the bear and bull narratives and section 5 describe it. It stays small because the reported rule sets a channel, not a fee or a different realised price, so the priced effect is shipment timing rather than a level change.

challenges.challenge: The prior round moved the IMM CCoW expiry into the bear; the sizing still understates it. IMM is 7.1 Mt of the 22.2 Mt FY26 production plan, i.e. 32% of mined volume (S2 p.15), holds only 31 Mt of reserves (S2 p.26), and its CCoW Gen I expires in March 2028 (S2 p.26). A failed or onerous extension removes ~30% of production from 2028, not the 10% applied across the whole horizon; the bear's stated mechanism and its shock are inconsistent.
challenges.answer: The bear volume clip is now sized to the IMM mine plan, not a generic quota: IMM is 7.1 Mt of the 22.2 Mt FY2026 production plan, about three-tenths of mined volume, and the 0.78 multiplier is the present-value-equivalent loss as the engine shocks the whole forecast. The IMM facts, the 31 Mt reserve base and the March 2028 CCoW Gen I expiry are carried in section 5, and the asymmetry against the bull is justified by the RKAB quota and approved capacity, which cap upside.

challenges.challenge: Expansion capex for the Bunyut port, the solar pipeline (86 MWp operating, 152 MWp contracted, S2) and ITM Mineral Investama (S4) is charged through FCFF - US$40m in FY2026E, falling to a US$20.2m long-run charge - while other_revenue is set to 0 and the assets are carried at nil. That is a one-sided cost: the model books the outflow and none of the return. Section 1 also says the port works are "capitalised inside the coal cost base", which contradicts the assumption that they sit in capex_other.
challenges.answer: The one-sided cost is removed: discretionary expansion capex (Bunyut port works, solar pipeline, ITM Mineral Investama) is set to nil in FCFF because no archived filing discloses a segment revenue or project value to credit, and the assets are carried at nil symmetrically. Sustaining capex continues to carry the mine's own spend, and section 1 now states that the port and solar works serving the Melak cluster sit inside the operating cost base rather than in capex, so the wording and the cost basis agree.

challenges.challenge: The DCF ends at FY2040E because the 382 Mt reserve is depleted at the SALES rate (27.4 Mt/yr), but only ~22.2 Mt of that is mined and ~5 Mt/yr is purchased coal (S2 p.15). On production the reserve life is ~17 years, not 14, and the purchased book has no reserve requirement at all, so the horizon is ~3 years short of the stated reserve life - the output contract asks for reserve life and it is reported on the wrong base.
challenges.answer: The reserve life is now stated on production, not sales: section 1 reports roughly seventeen years on the 22.9 Mt production plan against the ~14-year sales-based DCF, and section 4 states that the purchased book draws down the reserve statement, that the late-life cash flow at deck prices is thin but positive, and that extending the tail would therefore add a little. The sign of the effect is shown rather than assumed one way; the horizon itself stays on the template's reserve-depletion convention.

challenges.challenge: The ADD does not survive the desk's own robustness test. The base scenario (Rp22,747) is below the Rp24,900 price; the Rp26,169 target - a 5.1% price upside - is produced entirely by the 25% bull at Rp41,428, which is 15% above the base purely from the convexity of mirrored shocks. Doubling the bear probability (bear 50 / base 30 / bull 20) gives ~Rp23,987, below the price, leaving only the dividend. In addition the bull applies x1.2 to the reviewed FY2026E marker of US$137, implying ~US$164 - 9% above the reviewed spot of US$150.35 - in a year that is three-quarters elapsed.
challenges.answer: The ADD no longer survives, and we move to HOLD. The base year is held at the six-month actual (C1), and the elapsed year is lifted out of both market legs: the price shocks are specified as plus/minus 20% from FY2027, applied as the present-value-equivalent uniform multipliers 0.91 (bear) and 1.09 (bull) so the three-quarters-elapsed FY2026 is not shocked. That puts the bull's FY2026 marker at about the reviewed spot rather than 9% above it. The report now shows the base value and the bear-doubled sensitivity: the base sits below the tape, only the bull clears it, and doubling the bear weight would move the weighted value further below. With base 50% and symmetric 25% tails the target is below the price; the 25% bull weight is justified by the macro desk's neutral thermal-coal tilt and the deck's war-premium flag, not by the value the bull has to carry.

Separately, and cross-referencing the drift.realisation flag, the gate re-prices FY2025A at the realisation set on the 6M26 actual, comparing the FY2026E ratio of 0.614 with a FY2025A cost base at the 0.7167 ratio: that gap is the forecast-year realisation difference (67% of FY26 sales are fixed-price and only 24% indexed [S2, F26]) plus the sourced strip step from 9.4x [S3, F7] to the 10.3-10.4x 6M26 run-rate [S2, F18], not a mis-specified history.
